# The Hateful Immortals

## A Partial Documentary History of the Greenbriar-Chen Marriage (1847–Present)

### Compiled, Annotated, and Introduced by Dr. Amelia Thornton
#### Hargrove Chair in Anomalous Longitudinal Studies, Radcliffe Institute for Advanced Study

---

A note on method.

I am aware that the phrase "anomalous longitudinal studies" strikes most of my colleagues in the conventional social sciences as either a polite euphemism or an outright joke. I have been introduced at conferences as "the woman who interviews the impossible" and, on one occasion that I will not dignify with additional context, as "Harvard's most expensive ghost hunter." I accept these characterizations in the spirit in which they are offered, which is to say, not graciously. My credentials are a matter of public record: doctorate in comparative social history, Columbia, 1996; postdoctoral fellowship in archival methodology, the Sorbonne, 1998; seventeen years of fieldwork across four continents; and a security clearance from an agency I am contractually forbidden from naming but which, I can confirm, maintains a file on the subjects of this monograph that is thicker than the Manhattan telephone directory was in the year it ceased publication.

I mention all of this not out of vanity—though I am told I possess that quality in adequate supply—but because the evidentiary claims I am about to make require the reader to accept, at least provisionally, that I am neither a fabulist nor a fool. What follows is drawn from primary documents, recorded interviews, municipal records, medical reports, and, in several cases, physical artifacts that are currently held in a climate-controlled vault at an institution I am not authorized to name but which is not, despite persistent rumor, located beneath the Widener Library.

We begin with a daguerreotype.

---

**I.**

The image measures approximately two and three-quarters by three and a quarter inches. It is housed in a Union case of thermoplastic, embossed with a floral motif consistent with manufacture in the Boston area between 1845 and 1850. The plate itself is in remarkable condition—the silver surface exhibits only minimal tarnish along the lower left margin, a preservation anomaly that is consistent with having been stored for decades in a cedar-lined box that Margaret Greenbriar, née Aldworth, has described in interview as "the only piece of furniture I have never once considered leaving behind."

The image depicts two figures seated before a painted backdrop of classical columns. Their clothing is formal but not extravagant: he wears a dark frock coat and cravat; she wears a dress of what she has identified, from memory, as "dove-gray silk with a pagoda sleeve that I detested even at the time but which my mother insisted was appropriate for the occasion." They are young. They appear, by the conventions of physiological assessment, to be in their early twenties. They are, in fact, both twenty-three years old. They will both appear to be twenty-three years old when this document is published, an interval of one hundred and seventy-seven years that I note here not for dramatic effect but because the number itself is the only honest abstract of the evidence I have spent the better part of my career collecting.

Their names are Margaret Greenbriar and James Chen.

The marriage license, filed with the Suffolk County Clerk's Office on the fourteenth of June, 1847, identifies the groom as James Wending Chen, merchant, age twenty-three, resident of Beacon Hill. It identifies the bride as Margaret Rose Aldworth, age twenty-three, of Brookline. The document bears the signatures of both parties and of two witnesses: a Mr. Harold Fitch, since identified as James's business partner in a modest import concern that operated out of Long Wharf, and a Miss Constance Aldworth, Margaret's younger sister, who was seventeen at the time and whose subsequent correspondence with Margaret constitutes one of the primary documentary sources for the early decades of the marriage.

The license has never been annulled, voided, dissolved, or superseded. It predates the first no-fault divorce statute in any American jurisdiction by one hundred and twenty-two years. It predates the California Family Law Act of 1969 by one hundred and twenty-two years, the Uniform Marriage and Divorce Act by one hundred and twenty-three, and, for that matter, the ratification of the Fourteenth Amendment by twenty-one. I mention these legal milestones not to suggest that the Greenbriar-Chen marriage has endured because divorce was unavailable—both parties have confirmed, with considerable feeling, that they have investigated the legal options in every era and in multiple countries—but to establish a fact that the reader will need to hold in mind throughout. This marriage has outlasted every legal, social, and cultural framework that existed at the time of its formation. It has outlasted the institution of slavery, the Ottoman Empire, the gold standard, and the concept of a party-line telephone. It has persisted through thirty-three American presidential administrations. I enumerate these landmarks because the human mind, including my own, tends to slide off the surface of a number like one hundred and seventy-seven, and I wish the reader to feel, even briefly, the texture of the time this number contains.

Now. The hands.

Daguerreotype exposure times in 1847 typically ranged from fifteen to sixty seconds, depending on available light and plate chemistry. The photographic record shows that James Chen's hands are perfectly rendered: crisp, sharp, folded in his lap with a stillness that the eye registers as composure but that is, given what we know of his physiology, something more accurately described as constitutional. His body does not fidget because his body does not experience the minor muscular discomforts—the fatigue, the itch, the restless nerve—that make ordinary people shift in their chairs. He sat still for sixty seconds because he could have sat still for sixty years.

Margaret's right hand is blurred. It is a faint smear of light at her side, a small ghost of motion in an otherwise frozen composition. She moved during the exposure. She has confirmed this. "I was thinking about the soup," she told me in our first interview, in 2019, with an expression I can only describe as deeply inconvenienced by the question. "Not the metaphysical implications of being photographed for the first time. Constance had made a chowder and left it on the stove, and I remember—of course I remember—wondering whether it would scorch. I can still smell that studio. Copper and lavender water and Mr. Alcott's hair pomade. And the chowder, which did scorch, and which Constance never entirely forgave me for, and which I can describe to you at a molecular level if you have four hours and no commitment to remaining interested."

I record this digression because it is illustrative. Margaret Greenbriar's anomalous capacity—I follow the terminology established by the federal interagency report of 2004, which I helped draft and which no one has read—manifests as total, permanent, multisensory recall of every experience she has undergone since the capacity's emergence at age thirteen. She does not possess an exceptional memory. She possesses an *absolute* one. Every conversation, every ambient sound, every quality of light, every temperature reading of every room she has ever entered is preserved at original fidelity and is accessible to conscious recall without degradation, distortion, or decay. She remembers the chowder with the same clarity that she remembers, as I will later document, the smell of James's blood on a kitchen floor in Buenos Aires in 1923. Her neurology draws no distinction between the trivial and the catastrophic. It keeps everything. It discards nothing.

James Chen's anomalous capacity, which emerged at age fourteen, is of an entirely different character. His body is biologically indestructible. It can be damaged—extensively, grotesquely, in ways that I will catalogue later and that I recommend the squeamish reader prepare for—but it will, in every documented instance, restore itself to its baseline state. Broken bones re-fuse. Burned tissue regenerates. Severed vessels re-anastomose. He has been clinically dead, by any reasonable definition of the term, on at least fourteen occasions that I have been able to verify. He always comes back. He comes back as himself, at twenty-three, without scarring, without cellular degradation, and, as far as can be determined by the neurological examinations he has grudgingly submitted to, without any structural change to his brain.

This last point is significant.

They met in the autumn of 1846 at a public lecture on phrenology delivered by a Dr. Ezekiel Brunt at the Boston Athenaeum. Margaret was accompanied by Constance. James was alone. Both attended under the same private hope: that the emerging science of cranial measurement might offer some explanation—any explanation—for what had happened to them. Margaret, in a 2003 interview with my predecessor Dr. Hannigan, described the lecture as "forty-five minutes of confident nonsense during which a man with regrettable sideburns claimed he could diagnose moral character by fondling skulls." She then added, without change of tone: "James was sitting three rows ahead of me and to the left. He was wearing a brown coat. The seat creaked when he leaned forward. He leaned forward exactly twice—once when Dr. Brunt mentioned the organ of Marvelousness, and again when a woman in the front row asked whether phrenology might account for physical anomalies. I knew he was like me before he turned around. I knew from the way he leaned."

They were introduced at the reception following the lecture. They married eleven months later. The intervening courtship is documented primarily through Margaret's letters to Constance, which are held in the collection I mentioned and which I have been granted limited access to under conditions of temperature, humidity, and supervisory presence that I found excessive but complied with. I will quote here from a letter dated March 7, 1847, approximately three months before the wedding:

*He is the only person alive who understands what it is to be permanently strange. I do not mean that he understands my particular strangeness—he does not, and I suspect he never shall, as his mind does not work as mine does and he finds my descriptions of it either fascinating or unsettling depending on the hour. But he knows the shape of the condition. He knows what it is to sit in a room full of people and to be, irrevocably, not one of them. I did not know, before I met him, that this loneliness had a cure. I am not certain it does. But he is the nearest thing to one I have found, and I will take the nearest thing over the alternative, which is nothing.*

This is, by any measure, a remarkable letter. It is also, by Margaret's own retrospective assessment, a deeply embarrassing one. In 2019, when I read the passage aloud during our joint interview at the couple's current residence—a mildly depressing condominium in Portland, Oregon, which I will describe at a later juncture—Margaret sat without expression for approximately four seconds and then said: "That is the most naïve sentence I have ever produced."

James, who was reading a magazine in the adjacent armchair during this exchange, said, without looking up: "Which one?"

"'The only person alive who understands what it is to be permanently strange,'" Margaret said.

"Ah," James said. He turned a page.

"Do you disagree?" I asked.

He appeared to consider this. "I think," he said, "that she was right at the time, and that she was wrong eventually, and that the part in between is what a marriage is."

Margaret looked at him for a long moment. I recorded the duration: seven seconds. Then she said, "That is the most intelligent thing you've said in a decade."

"Give it time," James said. "You'll ruin it by remembering it."

I noted then, and I note again here for the reader's benefit, that this is the paradox on which the entire documented history of the Greenbriar-Chen marriage turns. She remembers everything. He endures everything. These are not, as one might casually assume, complementary capacities. They are, as the subsequent evidence will show, fundamentally opposed ones—two different relationships to time, to loss, and to the accumulation of experience, yoked together by a Suffolk County marriage license and one hundred and seventy-seven years of what Margaret has described variously as "stubbornness," "pathology," and, on one occasion, "the greatest and most wretched love affair in the history of the species, which no one will ever appreciate because it is also the most tedious."

We proceed.

---

**II.**

In a 1987 interview conducted by Dr. Patricia Yoon—a clinical psychologist who held the Hargrove Chair before Hannigan, and whose interview transcripts I have reviewed in their entirety—Margaret was asked to identify the first significant argument of the marriage. She responded by distinguishing, at length and with evident irritation, between "significant" and "first." "We argued before breakfast on the second day," she said. "He left his shaving brush on the washstand in a way that seemed, to me, deliberately inconsiderate. That was the first argument. It was not significant. The significant one came later."

"When?" Dr. Yoon asked.

"1852. November. A Tuesday. Seven-forty in the evening, approximately. The fire had burned low. The room was fifty-eight degrees. I know this because I was cold, and I remember precisely what fifty-eight degrees feels like against the exposed skin of my forearms, which were exposed because I had rolled my sleeves to rearrange the furniture."

I note for the reader that Dr. Yoon's handwritten marginalia in the transcript at this point reads: *Patient states date, day, time, and ambient temperature of argument that occurred 135 years ago. No apparent effort of recall. Verify?* The question mark is heavily underscored.

Margaret's account of the argument is as follows:

James had been traveling—a trip to New York on business related to the import concern, which by 1852 had expanded to include textile brokerage. He had been gone for nine days. Margaret, alone in their rented house on Pinckney Street, had reorganized the parlor. She moved the settee to the opposite wall, rehung the curtains, and replaced the arrangement of dried flowers on the mantelpiece with a small framed print of Gloucester Harbor that she had purchased from a street vendor. Her account of the vendor—his height, his accent (she identifies it as Dorchester), the chipped button on his left cuff, the quality of the light on Tremont Street at 2:15 in the afternoon on November 14, 1852—is consistent with her documented recall capacity and occupies nearly a full page of Dr. Yoon's transcript before Dr. Yoon gently redirects her to the argument.

James returned. He entered the parlor. Margaret reports that he set his bag down—a leather portmanteau, brown, with a scratch on the left clasp that had been there since 1849—and looked at the rearranged room. There was a pause of what she estimates as four seconds. Then he said:

"You might have consulted me, as it is my home as well."

Margaret, in the 1987 interview, recites this sentence with a particular and specific inflection. Dr. Yoon's transcript notes: *Subject reproduces apparent vocal quality of spouse, including pitch, cadence, and emphasis pattern. Emphasis falls on "consulted" and "as well." Subject states that spouse's left hand was at his side, slightly curled, not quite a fist.* Margaret told Dr. Yoon that she replied, at the time: "I might have, had you been here."

She then paused—in 1987, not in 1852; this is the kind of temporal distinction the reader must become comfortable with—and said: "That was an unremarkable exchange by any standard. Marriage is made of such sentences. A wife rearranges the furniture; a husband objects; both forget it by supper."

"But you didn't forget it," Dr. Yoon said.

"Dr. Yoon," Margaret said, "I don't forget anything. That is what I have been telling you for the past three hours."

"What I mean—"

"I know what you mean. You mean: did it trouble me. And the answer is that it didn't, for approximately five years. It was a sentence. It sat in the place where all my sentences sit, which is everywhere, always, at full volume, and it was no more prominent than the ten thousand other sentences James had spoken to me that year. He said it. I heard it. The fire was low. The room was fifty-eight degrees."

"And then?"

"And then it was 1857, and James accepted a position with a shipping firm without discussing it with me first. And I was standing in the kitchen of our new house—we had moved to Charlestown by then—and I heard it again. Not 'remembered' it, Dr. Yoon. *Heard* it. The same tone. The same pitch.
